title: The Computer That Would Think: Japan's Fifth Generation Project, 1982–1992
search_title: Japan's Fifth Generation Computer project 1982–1992: the plan, the panic, the result
description: In 1982, Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry launched a ten-year national programme to build a computer that could reason, converse in natural language, and leapfrog Western computing entirely. The announcement set off a global alarm, triggering rival programmes in the United States, Britain, and Europe. This essay traces the plan's origins in the mind of a mid-level bureaucrat, the genuine technical achievements of ICOT, and why a project that met most of its own goals came to be remembered as a failure.
standfirst: In October 1981, Japan told the world it was going to build a computer that thinks. What happened next was less a technology race than a mirror in which every participant saw a different threat.
body:
## Tokyo, October 1981 The invitations arrived unsolicited at computer science departments around the world. Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry was convening an international conference in Tokyo to present, for comment and collaboration, a plan for the next generation of computing. The gesture was unusual: MITI's previous technology initiatives had been launched with little English-language fanfare, aimed at domestic industry rather than international audiences.1 This one was different. Around three hundred people attended, representing fourteen countries, including the American expert-systems pioneer Edward Feigenbaum, who had been invited to speak.2 What the visitors encountered was, by the standards of a computing conference, bewildering. A lengthy conceptual diagram of the proposed system, reproduced throughout the conference materials for years afterward, showed layers of hardware and software of considerable complexity, connecting natural-language interfaces to knowledge bases to parallel inference engines to relational databases. Many attendees found the materials, as one put it, "rather obscure."3 The conference keynote was delivered by Toru Moto-oka, a professor of electrical engineering at the University of Tokyo who chaired the planning committee. He stated Japan's intention to be a full partner in the international scientific community and called for future cooperation. Feigenbaum concluded his own talk by calling for international cooperation.4 Then the visitors went home. Back in their respective capitals, they did not cooperate. They panicked. ## The Dream The idea had begun not in a government ministry or a university laboratory but, as the cultural critic Jun'ichiro Uemae describes in his Japanese-language retrospective *Japanizu Dorimu*, over a few heady afternoons in 1978 in the office of a mid-level MITI manager named Masataka Nakano, then only thirty years old, who ran a handful of young programmers as a division chief on the fourth-generation VLSI project.5 Nakano's concern was not primarily about computing power. He was not a programmer and had no technical background; he was therefore, as the historian Colin Garvey notes in his account of the project, keenly aware of the social cost of computerisation in the Japanese office.6 Computers of the late 1970s were enormous machines requiring specialised training. Most government officials at MITI could not use them. Computer interfaces, where they were not purely numerical, were in English: Japanese users had to acquire a non-trivial amount of English on top of the technical knowledge itself, a considerable barrier. The result was that rather than streamlining the Japanese office, computers were adding to its burden. There was a geopolitical dimension as well. IBM dominated the international computer market by volume and through users' need for backward compatibility. Even competitors who built technically superior machines found that potential customers replied that if the machines could not run existing IBM software, they could not use them.7 Nakano saw this as locking Japan into an endless cycle of imitation. He wanted to break it. As Uemae records his words to his team: "This is why Japan has to be first to build a non-von Neumann machine. If we do, then we can race down an original path, outside of the world controlled by IBM."8 This was the seed of the Fifth Generation. Its name followed the accepted lineage of computing hardware: vacuum tubes (first generation), transistors (second), integrated circuits (third), microprocessors (fourth).9 The fifth would be something categorically different: machines that operated not on sequential numerical instructions but on logical inference, in parallel, accepting natural-language input from ordinary users. Nakano himself was rotated to a new post in another MITI division in 1979, just as the formal planning committee formed. Two-year rotations were, as Uemae notes, an entirely ordinary feature of Japanese working life. His name consequently does not appear in the official FGCS literature.10 The planning committee that emerged from his idea was chaired by Moto-oka and included three subcommittees, on Basic Theory, Computer Architecture, and Social Impacts, led respectively by Kazuhiro Fuchi, Hideo Aiso, and Hajime Karatsu.11 Around one hundred representatives from science, industry, and government participated in as many meetings over two years. The committee's ambitions were social as much as technical. As Karatsu's Social Impacts subcommittee set out in its preliminary report, the Fifth Generation computer would increase productivity in low-productivity areas, meet international competition by augmenting rather than replacing Japan's skilled labour force, assist in saving energy and resources, and help cope with an ageing society.12 Chairman Moto-oka later summarised the aspiration as a "Quantum Jump in Friendliness": a computer that fits the needs of people instead of making people work by the rules of the machine.13 What the committee explicitly did not call it was an artificial intelligence project. The Japanese term *jinkō chinō*, artificial intelligence, was American in origin and American in flavour. What ICOT would pursue was *chishiki jōhō shori shisutemu*: knowledge information processing systems. The distinction mattered to the planners. As Fuchi later asserted, responding to those who conflated the Fifth Generation with American AI: "our project is not an artificial intelligence project or an expert system project as wrongly understood by some people."14 ## The Wager In April 1982, MITI formally launched the project, establishing ICOT as a joint venture between the ministry and eight of Japan's largest computer and electronics manufacturers: Fujitsu, Hitachi, NEC, Toshiba, Mitsubishi Electric, Matsushita, Oki Electric, and Sharp.15 The institute opened in Tokyo under the direction of Kazuhiro Fuchi, who came from MITI's own Electrotechnical Laboratory. To the laboratory came forty young engineers and scientists, most in their twenties, from those eight firms.16 The project was to run for ten years in three phases: an initial stage focused on basic research (1982–1984), an intermediate stage on subsystems (1985–1988), and a final stage on complete prototype systems (1989–1992). The total investment ran to approximately ¥54 billion over the eleven fiscal years of the programme's operation, a figure confirmed by the Information Processing Society of Japan's Computer Museum and by Akira Ishikawa's 1993 retrospective at the University of Texas.17 The technical wager at the heart of the project rested on two linked bets. The first was that the correct language for the fifth generation kernel was Prolog, a logic programming language developed in Europe by Robert Kowalski and collaborators, rather than Lisp, the American AI community's standard tool.18 Fuchi had been impressed by logic programming on visits abroad and saw it as the "missing link" between knowledge information processing and the non-von Neumann hardware he intended to build. His choice of Prolog drew the ire of the American AI community: one influential commentator remarked that "Prolog is seen as somehow 'un-American' — a European fad that has now been taken up by the Japanese."19 Fuchi defended the choice by arguing that Prolog was technically superior and that Japan, as a newcomer, had no obligation to adopt the legacy language Lisp.20 The second bet was on massive parallelism. Performance targets were set in a project-specific unit, LIPS, Logical Inferences Per Second. Where a typical workstation of the early 1980s ran Prolog at roughly 100,000 LIPS, the project aimed for 100 million to 1 billion LIPS: three to four orders of magnitude of improvement, to be achieved by designing special-purpose parallel hardware from scratch.21 The industry participants were not enthusiastic. When they learned that Fuchi's plan had been approved and that the Fifth Generation computers would not be IBM-compatible, the eight firms attempted to back out of the project entirely.22 MITI applied pressure by threatening exclusion from future government funding opportunities, and industry eventually relented, though the companies never agreed to match funds as MITI had initially stipulated. Instead, they conceded to sending researchers on a rotating basis to ICOT.23 Fuchi accepted the directorship of ICOT on two conditions, both radical within Japanese business culture: that he could choose any computer manufacturer to provide terminals during the initial phase, including American machines, and that researchers seconded to ICOT were to be under thirty-five years old.24 He then signalled his intention to run the institute as an autonomous research institution free from commercial pressure, by regularly and painstakingly emphasising that the project had "no commercial objectives."25 Results were to be shared openly: published in scientific articles and conference presentations, in English as well as Japanese. ICOT would be a global research hub. As Fuchi put it, the project "must not be exclusive or closed to outsiders."26 ## The Panic The Western response to the 1981 Tokyo conference was immediate and, in the United States particularly, alarmed. The announcement came, as Feigenbaum and his Stanford colleague Howard Shrobe observed in a survey of the project written around 1987, "on the heels of MITI's highly successful efforts to promote Japanese prowess in consumer electronics and computer chips," and it "set off alarm bells in capitals and companies of the West."27 Britain moved first. A UK Department of Industry mission had attended the Tokyo conference, and its participants returned with a new assessment: rather than collaboration with the Japanese, there was "an urgent need for the U.K. to form its own fifth-generation computing strategy."28 The British government convened a committee under John Alvey, then head of R&D at British Telecom, which produced a report proposing a collaborative government-industry research programme. The result was the Alvey Programme, launched in May 1983, which the *Financial Times* announced under the headline "Britain Enters the Great Race."29 The United States followed a different logic. Feigenbaum, who had called for international cooperation at the Tokyo conference, returned home and began travelling the country giving seminars to computer scientists and government officials. His argument took book form in 1983 as *The Fifth Generation: Artificial Intelligence and Japan's Computer Challenge to the World*, co-authored with Pamela McCorduck and published by Addison-Wesley.30 The authors were frank that they were "decidedly not disinterested observers," and the book's conclusion called on Americans to mount a large-scale national project because failure to respond would mean consigning "our nation to the role of the first great postindustrial agrarian society."31 The book proved highly successful and widely influential, and was even a bestseller in Japan.32 Feigenbaum then testified before Congress in June 1983. He warned that the era of "reasoning machines is inevitable. It is the 'manifest destiny' of computing," and offered three options: a coordinated national response, an ICOT-like centre, or nothing and disaster.33 Congress embraced the alarm. Two major American programmes followed. The Microelectronics and Computer Technology Corporation, a for-profit industrial consortium of thirteen corporations, was founded in September 1983. DARPA's Strategic Computing Initiative, a decade-long, $1 billion project to create AI systems for each branch of the military, was signed by President Reagan in December 1983.34 There is a detail worth dwelling on. Robert Cooper, the DARPA director, and Robert Kahn, director of DARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office, had both attended the 1981 Tokyo conference. They returned, according to the historians Alex Roland and Philip Shiman, with a quite different impression: the Japanese were still trailing the United States in computing and were headed down a dead-end. This analysis did not stop them from exploiting Feigenbaum's alarmism. In later interviews, Cooper confessed to trundling out the Japanese "as the arch-enemies" and using the alarm "unabashedly" in private conversations with members of Congress.35 Europe joined the race with the European Strategic Programme on Research in Information Technology, ESPRIT, funded at nearly $2 billion over five years. The EEC's own minister, addressing a conference in the Netherlands, put it this way: "In information technology, the last boat is leaving. Europe has got to be on it."36 What happened in each capital is plain enough. The West did not replicate ICOT. It built something different in its image. Where ICOT was organised around shared research with published results and no commercial objectives, the American Microelectronics and Computer Technology Corporation almost immediately "shrouded much of its research in secrecy to protect shareholder advantage," resulting, as the *IEEE Spectrum* reported, in forced "isolation between projects" that undermined the potential benefits of cooperation.37 The Strategic Computing Initiative was explicitly military in aim. The Alvey Programme was decentralised across universities and firms rather than concentrated in a single institute, and it funded companies on commercial terms. ## What Was Actually Built Phase One of ICOT's work ran from 1982 to March 1985 and focused on logic programming. An early model of logic processing hardware was designed by ICOT and manufactured by Mitsubishi: a minicomputer workstation called PSI, the Personal Sequential Inference machine. A faster version, PSI-2, followed; a high-speed version called CHI was built by NEC for ICOT.38 ICOT extended and reworked Prolog into a powerful programming tool in which the operating software of their machines could be written, an effort that Feigenbaum and Shrobe noted in their survey of the project "resulted in the largest Prolog program by far ever written."39 Then Phase One ended in March 1985 and, in accordance with the staffing plan, almost everyone except Fuchi and his cadre of group managers rotated back to the member companies, replaced by new initiates. On a single day, a highly trained team of by then forty-eight technical people whose collective skill was ICOT's own knowledge base evaporated and was replaced by new initiates. To a Western research manager visiting at the time, what they did was incomprehensible.40 Phase Two produced the Parallel Inference Machine, or PIM: clusters of PSI machines running logic programs in parallel. Phase Three, the final stage, produced five architecturally distinct PIM models, PIM/p with 512 processing elements, PIM/m with 256, PIM/c, PIM/i, and PIM/k, used to run and evaluate a substantial body of demonstration software in domains including molecular biology, legal reasoning, and logic circuit design.41 Speedups of 50 to 100 times over conventional machines were achieved at configurations of around 500 processing elements. The project also developed KL1, a concurrent logic programming language, and PIMOS, an operating system for the parallel inference machines, both written within ICOT. The Information Processing Society of Japan's Computer Museum records the final result plainly: the project produced the world's fastest and largest computer oriented toward knowledge information processing, with the PIM/p and PIM/m now preserved at the National Museum of Nature and Science in Tokyo.42 The final evaluation report, submitted in March 1993, gave correspondingly reasonable marks on the question of goal attainment. Most technical goals were met. Almost no industrial legacy survived. ## Why It Failed, and Why That Question Is Complicated The word "failure" attached itself to the Fifth Generation so quickly and thoroughly that it is now difficult to assess the project without first noticing that the verdict was partly imported from outside. As the researchers Ehud Shapiro and David Warren, both of whom worked on the project, observed in a retrospective published in 1993, the West had perceived Japan as "promising to make the dream of artificial intelligence come true", claims that were "further amplified by scientists around the world, who capitalized on the fear of Japanese technological supremacy in order to scare their own governments into funding research."43 When Japanese computers had not dominated the global economy by the early 1990s, many in the West judged the project a failure by the standard of goals that the project itself had never set. Fuchi noted the resulting Catch-22 with some bitterness. An exaggerated image of the project was engendered early and seemed to persist, he wrote: the project first had to face criticism "that it was a reckless project trying to tackle impossible goals" and then criticism "that the project has failed because it has been unable to realize those grand goals."44 There was, however, a genuine technical problem, and it was not Japan's alone. The core bet of the Fifth Generation, that inference grounded in symbolic logic was the road to machine intelligence, was the mainstream view in AI research worldwide in the 1980s. Over the same decade, general-purpose processors improved in performance and fell in price at a pace that nobody anticipated. By the time the PIM hardware was complete, RISC workstations and Intel-based PCs had overtaken purpose-built inference machines on price-performance. A user had no reason to pay the double cost of special-purpose hardware and a wholesale change of programming model.45 This was not a uniquely Japanese miscalculation. DARPA's Strategic Computing Initiative "did not quite end; it simply disappeared," having "vanished" from the DARPA budget by 1993, in Roland and Shiman's account.46 The American market for special-purpose AI hardware collapsed in 1987. The Alvey Programme concluded in 1987 with mixed results, by the assessment of the evaluation carried out by the Universities of Manchester and Sussex.47 What Daniel Crevier, in his history of AI, called the "Rollercoaster of the 1980s" resulted in near-total collapse by the end of the decade across all the major programmes.48 There was also what the post-project assessments identified as a specifically Japanese institutional problem. ICOT had no permanent research staff: it was composed entirely of secondees from companies, turning over en masse at each stage boundary. Institutional memory was very difficult to accumulate. When the project concluded in 1992, no permanent entity existed anywhere with responsibility for bridging the results into commercial products. Real technical output existed, papers, working parallel inference machine prototypes, but no route connecting that output to products and markets had been built into the design.49 On the other hand, the staffing model did produce a training effect that ICOT itself always regarded as its first and most important achievement. By the end of Phase One in 1985, ICOT managers counted approximately 1,000 trained engineers in the field, including ICOT researchers, engineers in the cooperating sections of member company laboratories, and engineers in the proprietary sections.50 This was, in the view of the MITI planners, always the primary goal. The project closed formally on 1 June 1992 with a concluding international conference in Tokyo. Between 1992 and 1994, ICOT released its software deliverables free of charge as ICOT Free Software, some 100 programmes including the PIMOS source code and KLIC, an implementation that translates the project's concurrent logic language KL1 into C, allowing it to run without special-purpose hardware. ## The Verdict and Its Distortions Compared to its Western counterparts, the verdict on the Fifth Generation is paradoxical. The SCI, MCC, Alvey, and ESPRIT are typically remembered as partial successes; Japan's project is remembered as an outright failure. The historian Daniel Crevier's framing is representative: whereas the SCI merely "disappointed its military sponsors," the Japanese, he claims, "fell far short of their objectives."51 The asymmetry in verdict is hard to explain without reference to the story Feigenbaum's book had fixed in place. ICOT met most of its own technical milestones. The SCI vanished from its budget. Alvey concluded years before the Fifth Generation finished. The American market for AI hardware collapsed two years before ICOT's final conference. On any neutral accounting, the programmes had roughly comparable records of technical achievement and commercial non-delivery. What the Fifth Generation did not deliver was the one thing it had explicitly not promised: commercial dominance of the global computing market. That goal was Feigenbaum's, not Fuchi's. MITI considered the project a success on its own merits, a view confirmed by Nakamura and Shibuya's 1996 analysis of Japanese technology policy.52 Economic payoff, as Feigenbaum and Shrobe conceded in their own 1993 evaluation of the project, was never among ICOT's stated goals.53 The deeper failure was one of the bet itself, shared with the entire field. Nobody in 1982, not Fuchi, not Moto-oka, not the DARPA planners, not the Alvey committee, foresaw that the mid-1990s would bring a personal computing revolution built on exactly the von Neumann architecture that the Fifth Generation had proposed to replace. As the leading University of Tokyo AI researcher Yutaka Matsuo later reflected: "I know there is no 'What if?' in history, but my dream is to imagine that if the Web had appeared 15 years earlier, Japan would be sitting where Silicon Valley is right now."54 The supposed failure left a long shadow in Japan. From roughly 1997 to 2002, Matsuo observed, AI was so taboo in Japanese computing circles that to use even the Japanese word for it, *jinkō chinō*, drew condemnation.55 ## What Remains The Fifth Generation project was the first national, large-scale AI research and development programme to be conducted without military funding or explicit commercial objectives, a fact that the historian Garvey describes as comparatively unique.56 Its results were published openly, in English as well as Japanese, and eventually released on the young internet. Hundreds of international researchers visited ICOT each year. It built genuine hardware, five PIM models, two of which are in a national museum, and contributed significantly to the field of concurrent logic programming. It was also, by any reasonable measure, a bet on the wrong approach, made at a moment when the whole field was betting the same way. The difference was that MITI's version of the bet was more visible, more explicitly national in its ambitions, and more thoroughly presented as a threat by people who had their own reasons to raise the alarm. When the bet failed, alongside all the Western bets made in response, only Japan was called the loser. Nakano, the civil servant who had the idea in 1978 and was then rotated out of the project before it began, was on a business trip in New York when the Tokyo conference of 1981 set the world computing community in motion. His name does not appear anywhere in the official literature. By the time the project closed in 1992, Fuchi and his colleagues had spent a decade being told they were building either a monster or a failure, depending on the year and the continent. The monster never appeared. The failure is harder to locate than the histories suggest. And the question of what it means for a government to commit ¥54 billion to a single technical bet, over a decade, with no way to change course if the bet goes wrong, that question, this essay's and not its sources', has not aged at all.
